column4: The section explicitly sets this command beside raised prophetic renown: believers must not let their own أَصْوَاتَكُمْ rise above صَوْتِ ٱلنَّبِىِّ, so the root ر ف ع becomes a boundary around the Prophet's audible voice.

The section explicitly makes this the inward pole of dhikr: the addressee remembers his Lord within himself, humbly and fearfully, دُونَ ٱلْجَهْرِ مِنَ ٱلْقَوْلِ, against the outwardly elevated sound of renown.
Moses asks God to loosen the knot in his tongue; this gives the section's passage from bodily strain to prophetic sound another concrete bodily site.
The purpose of the loosened tongue in 20:27 is that people understand قَوْلِى, making intelligible heard speech the outcome of bodily release.
Moses asks that Aaron strengthen أَزْرِى, his supporting strength or back; it is a close bodily counterpart to the back that creaks under a load in the section.
The support requested in 20:29-32 is to enable abundant glorification, كَىْ نُسَبِّحَكَ كَثِيرًا, joining relief of strain to voiced praise.
Moses adds وَنَذْكُرَكَ كَثِيرًا, so strengthened support and released speech culminate in the section's prayer-and-praise sense of dhikr.
Moses' prayer رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى restages the opening bodily relief of surah 94 and begins a sequence that ends in speech, glorification, and remembrance.
وَيَسِّرْ لِىٓ أَمْرِى asks for the task to be eased before the tongue is released, paralleling the movement from burden to ease and then to audible mission.
Moses asks that Aaron share his أَمْر, identifying the support of 20:31 as relief within the prophetic task rather than merely physical strength.
God will cast upon the Prophet قَوْلًا ثَقِيلًا, a weighty word; the revelation is simultaneously speech and a load capable of making a prophetic body strain.
Night rising is described as stronger in bodily impression and more upright in speech, أَقْوَمُ قِيلًا, joining exertion under weight to the formation of a sound.
وَٱذْكُرِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ وَتَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ makes remembrance of the Lord's name turn wholly toward Him, matching the section's inward turn at surah 94's close.
Good speech ascends to God and righteous action يَرْفَعُهُ; spoken words literally take the upward path that the section hears in raised dhikr and desire directed to the Lord.
Houses are permitted أَن تُرْفَعَ and God's name is remembered within them, وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا ٱسْمُهُ, bringing elevation and voiced remembrance into one scene.
Once riders settle on the animals' backs, ظُهُورِهِ, they remember their Lord's favor and speak a praise; saddle, back, dhikr, and human voice meet in one act.

Abraham is told to proclaim the pilgrimage to humanity, and the call brings riders on lean mounts from every distant pass; an elevated voice travels afar through the very caravan world evoked by the section's saddle-song.
God gives Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ عَلِيًّا, a lofty truthful tongue or renown, a direct Quranic image for a good name raised across distance and generations.
Abraham asks for لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ فِى ٱلْـَٔاخِرِينَ, truthful mention among later people; 19:50 answers the request and clarifies the enduring-voice sense of raised dhikr.
God and the angels bless the Prophet and believers are commanded to voice blessings and peace upon him; his honored mention is repeatedly carried by other voices.
Jesus announces a messenger to come after him whose name is أَحْمَدُ, staging the Prophet's name as a sound sent ahead of him through time.
At heard revelation, skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften toward ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ; remembrance becomes a sound registered inside the body, like the section's audible joints and ribs.
Job calls his Lord from bodily distress described as بِنُصْبٍ وَعَذَابٍ; this Quranic fatigue sense of ن ص ب meets both the section's straining body and its secondary song sense.
Moses' companion says the journey has brought them نَصَبًا; travel fatigue supplies the Quranic caravan-side counterpart to the lexicon's nasb song sung along a road.
Were the Quran laid upon a mountain, it would be seen humbled and cracked from fear; the word itself becomes a load that makes a body-like structure break under strain.
The heavens nearly rupture above while the angels glorify their Lord's praise; structural breaking and a sound of praise occur together, closely matching the section's passage from creak to dhikr.
The lost carry their burdens عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ; this literal load-on-backs scene supplies the dark counterpart to the Prophet's burden being removed.

A heavily laden soul calls out for help with its load, yet none of it is carried by another; the section's groan under weight becomes an explicit call, while divine relief in surah 94 reverses the refusal.
God knows that the Prophet's breast is constricted by what opponents say; hostile speech is experienced as bodily pressure before the next ayah turns him to praise.
The response to the constricted breast of 15:97 is to glorify the Lord's praise and prostrate, converting pressure caused by speech into prayer and praise.
The sequence continues from constriction and praise into sustained worship, giving the section's فَٱنصَبْ the same movement from released burden into devotion.
Zechariah's sign is that he cannot speak to people except by gesture, yet he is told to remember his Lord much and glorify morning and evening; ordinary voice falls silent while dhikr remains.
Zechariah is given a three-night inability to address people despite being sound; it establishes a bodily silence against which the next ayah's commanded praise is communicated.
Unable to speak, Zechariah gestures to his people that they should glorify morning and evening, showing praise conveyed at the edge of audible voice.
Zechariah calls his Lord نِدَآءً خَفِيًّا, a hidden or quiet call, a precise Quranic instance of supplication taking the inward sound-path described in the section.
The quiet caller reports weakened bones and old age; an inward prayer emerges from a failing body, sharpening the section's attention to the sounds of joints and ribs.
The Prophet is told neither to make his prayer loud nor wholly quiet but to seek a path between; this is the explicit vocal boundary between raised sound and inward remembrance.
Luqman tells his son to lower his voice and names the donkey's voice as the harshest; voice height and an animal sound, two dictionary strands developed in the section, meet directly.
Whether speech is made aloud or kept secret, God knows what is still more hidden; it preserves both ends of the section's audible-renown and inward-dhikr spectrum.
Voices are hushed before the Merciful until only a whisper is heard, supplying the low extreme against the section's sound that is raised and travels.
God is near and answers the caller's call; the inwardly directed supplication at the section's end does not require loudness in order to be heard.
The command to call the Lord humbly and secretly gives the supplication sense of dhikr a deliberately quiet vocal form.
The prophets call God رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا, in hope and fear; the same desire-root as surah 94's فَٱرْغَبْ is realized here as prayer voiced toward God.
Their sides leave their beds as they call their Lord in fear and hope; bodily exertion, inward desire, and prayer converge as they do at the end of surah 94.
God commands Moses to establish prayer لِذِكْرِى, making the section's dictionary statement that dhikr can be prayer explicit within an addressed prophetic command.
The successful person remembers the name of his Lord and then prays, فَصَلَّىٰ, placing named remembrance and ṣalāh in the same compact sequence.
After the promised opening and people entering the faith, the Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord's praise; completed work turns into voiced devotion just as in 94:7-8.
Once prayer is completed, believers are to remember God standing, sitting, and lying down; release from one act leads into embodied dhikr, closely paralleling فَإِذَا فَرَغْتَ فَٱنصَبْ.
The public call to Friday prayer summons believers to ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ, making dhikr at once an audible summons and the worship toward which it calls.
After the prayer is finished, believers disperse, seek God's bounty, and remember Him much; the after-completion structure directly illuminates the renewed exertion of 94:7.
When the call to prayer is sounded, opponents take it as mockery and play; an audible act of worship is heard but denied its honor, reversing raised and honored dhikr.
Birds with wings outspread join all creation in prayer and glorification, each knowing its ṣalāh and tasbīḥ; animal sound meets precisely the prayer-and-praise branch of dhikr.
Mountains and birds are commanded to echo or return praise with David; nonhuman sound becomes an answering song of glorification.
The mountains are subjected with David, glorifying at evening and sunrise; creation's sound is synchronized with a human prophet's praise.
The gathered birds are each أَوَّابٌ with David, completing 38:18's chorus and giving the section's animal-sound branch a devotional direction.
Mountains and birds are made to glorify with David; animal and landscape voices participate in the praise sense assigned to dhikr in the section.
Everything glorifies God's praise, though humans do not understand their glorification; the verse establishes meaningful nonhuman sound at the boundary of human hearing.
Solomon says that he and David were taught the speech of birds; the dictionary's eagle and chicken sounds become, in Quranic terms, an intelligible animal voice.
Solomon smiles at the ant's speech from 27:18 and immediately turns to a prayer of gratitude; heard animal voice becomes supplication directed to the Lord.
Every community is given a rite so that God's name is mentioned over the livestock He provides; animal bodies and voiced remembrance are joined in worship.
God's name is to be mentioned over the sacrificial camels while they stand in rows; a human sacred utterance sounds over the large animals evoked by saddles and caravan song.
Livestock carry people's loads to a land they could reach only with great bodily hardship; this is the Quran's clearest ordinary caravan scene behind the creaking saddle image.
The Quran is revealed to the Prophet so that he warn his hearers and whoever it reaches, وَمَنۢ بَلَغَ; prophetic utterance is explicitly destined to travel beyond its first audience.
A group of jinn attend the Prophet while he recites the Quran and tell one another to listen; his otherwise human voice reaches an unseen audience.
After hearing the recitation, the jinn name it a revealed book and carry its guidance onward, extending the first heard voice through new speakers.
God addresses the Prophet as witness, bearer of good news, and warner, roles enacted through the public voice whose reach the section hears in his raised mention.
The Prophet is specifically a caller to God, دَاعِيًا إِلَى ٱللَّهِ, so his elevated public sound has the same Godward direction as the section's final inward desire.
The Prophet is commanded to proclaim openly what he has been ordered; this is the outward mission-voice whose renown must travel beyond a private utterance.
The Prophet is told to proclaim his Lord's favor, فَحَدِّثْ, turning received relief into an audible account immediately before surah 94's burden-and-renown sequence.
The Prophet does not speak from personal desire; this distinguishes the authority of his audible speech from ordinary human voices that 49:2 must not place over it.
His utterance is identified as revelation conveyed to him, completing 53:3 and explaining why the prophetic voice bears exceptional weight and honor.
Believers are commanded to support and honor the Messenger and to glorify God morning and evening; prophetic honor and spoken praise are coordinated in one command.
The revealed book contains ذِكْرُكُمْ, which can be the addressees' reminder or their honor; that live ambiguity is the same remembrance-and-renown range the section hears in dhikr.
The Quran is called a ذِكْرٌ for the Prophet and his people, plausibly both reminder and honor for which they will answer, directly activating the section's paired senses.
God leaves something enduring for Noah among later peoples; the following salutation shows that what remains is an honorable spoken remembrance.
سَلَامٌ عَلَىٰ نُوحٍ فِى ٱلْعَـٰلَمِينَ voices Noah's name in peace throughout the worlds, completing the enduring mention of 37:78.
God leaves enduring mention for Abraham among later generations, answering Abraham's request in 26:84 for a truthful tongue after him.
سَلَامٌ عَلَىٰٓ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ makes the enduring mention of 37:108 audible by pronouncing Abraham's name in blessing.
God leaves enduring mention for Moses and Aaron among later generations, another explicit form of prophetic renown made to outlast the body.
سَلَامٌ عَلَىٰ مُوسَىٰ وَهَـٰرُونَ supplies the spoken names that complete the lasting remembrance announced in 37:119.
God leaves enduring mention for Elias among later generations, repeating the Quranic pattern of preserving a prophet through praised speech.
سَلَامٌ عَلَىٰٓ إِلْ يَاسِينَ voices the salutation that gives the enduring mention of 37:129 its audible form.
God did not teach the Prophet poetry; his utterance is instead ذِكْرٌ and clear Quran. This directly guards the section's lexical nasb-song echo from collapsing prophetic remembrance into song.
Opponents tell one another not to listen to the Quran and to make noise over it; their deliberate din tries to cover the revealed voice, reversing the listening discipline of 49:2.
The heavens nearly rupture, the earth splits, and mountains collapse under an asserted word; cosmic breaking amplifies the section's smaller creak of a body under pressure.
This ayah identifies the pressure-producing claim in 19:90 as attributing a child to the Merciful, so a spoken proposition rather than a physical load causes the rupture.
The heavens, earth, and mountains recoil from bearing the Trust, while the human being bears it; a refused cosmic load sets the scale for bodily strain under a moral charge.
The prayer asks God not to lay an iṣr upon the believers and not to make them carry what exceeds their capacity; divine removal of the Prophet's burden becomes a model for this requested relief.
The Messenger removes people's burdens and shackles, reversing the direction of surah 94: the one whose own load was removed becomes the means by which others are unburdened.
Whoever turns away from the revealed reminder given in 20:99 will carry a burden on resurrection; rejecting dhikr produces the very load that God removed from the Prophet.
The burden of 20:100 is an abiding and evil load, حِمْلًا, completing the reversal between receiving remembrance and being crushed by weight.
The people of the lasting abode say that no نَصَب touches them there; this negated fatigue marks the final boundary of the exertion commanded by فَٱنصَبْ.
Faces in the Fire are عَامِلَةٌ نَّاصِبَةٌ, laboring and exhausted; the same root turns devoted exertion into futile, punishing toil.
The Torah-bearer who does not bear its meaning is likened to a donkey carrying books; the laden animal gives the saddle-and-load scene a warning about carrying words without inward remembrance.
The woman who unravels her yarn after it was strong enacts the breaking branch of ن ق ض; it lets the creak named by the source lexicon hover at the edge of structural undoing.
The revelation is called the speech of a noble messenger, setting up the next ayah's denial that this elevated utterance is a poet's performance.
The messenger's utterance is not the word of a poet; like 36:69, this draws a firm boundary between revealed dhikr and the section's secondary song sense of nasb.
The poets are followed by the erring; this begins a boundary around song-like speech that 26:227 will reopen only for poetry joined to faith, action, and abundant remembrance.
The exception among poets includes those who believe, act rightly, and remember God much; poetic voice and dhikr may meet, but only under an explicit ethical boundary.
Believers must not make the Messenger's calling among them like their calling of one another; the Prophet's call and name receive a distinct audible status.
Those who lower their voices before the Messenger are praised, giving the positive form of the vocal limit stated in 49:2.
People call the Prophet from behind his chambers; the ayah censures a loud mode of reaching him and shows that not every extension of his name honors him.
Waiting silently until the Prophet comes out would be better than the calls of 49:4, making restraint itself part of the scene's proper treatment of voice.
Whether people conceal their speech or make it public, God knows what breasts contain; inward and outward sound are held within one divine hearing.
Believers' hearts tremble when God is mentioned and their faith grows when His ayat are recited; heard sacred speech has a bodily resonance.
Hearts find rest through remembrance of God, giving the inward bodily resolution of the section's movement away from a back strained by weight.
The humble are those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned and who patiently bear what befalls them; voiced remembrance and endurance under affliction meet.
Hearts are called to become humble at God's remembrance and revealed truth; dhikr is heard deeply enough to alter the body within.
An ant audibly warns its community of Solomon's approaching host; its small animal voice is the specific sound that Solomon hears and answers with prayer in 27:19.
The riders' spoken praise in 43:13 ends by saying that they will return to their Lord, matching the section's turn of sound and desire toward God.
The command to mention Idris in the Book preserves his name in recited scripture; the next ayah then distinguishes this textual remembrance from raising the prophet himself.
God raises Idris to a high station, وَرَفَعْنَـٰهُ مَكَانًا عَلِيًّا; beside 19:56, it contrasts raising a prophet with raising a prophet's mention.
The command to mention Mary in the Book makes recited revelation a vehicle by which a human name is carried beyond its first time and place.
The command to mention Abraham in the Book realizes his later truthful renown through repeated recitation of his name.
Moses is to be mentioned in the Book as a chosen messenger and prophet, giving honorable remembrance a durable textual voice.
Ishmael is to be mentioned in the Book and praised for fidelity, so named remembrance functions as the honor sense identified in the source section.
After the rites, people are to remember God as they remembered their forefathers or more intensely; divine dhikr redirects the public recitation of ancestral names.
The Prophet is told to recite the Quran in measured recitation; this gives the weighty word of 73:5 its disciplined audible form.
The enwrapped Prophet is told to rise and warn, turning bodily rising into the public voice of his mission.
Immediately after rising to warn, he is told to magnify his Lord; proclamation turns into praise, as the section's outward and Godward sound paths do.
The best speech belongs to one who calls to God and acts rightly; a voice gains elevation through its Godward direction and the deed accompanying it.
A protected outsider is to be brought near until he hears God's word; recited revelation is presented as an audible message capable of reaching a new hearer.
The jinn report that they heard a wondrous Quran, another scene in which the Prophet's recitation travels beyond the visible human audience.
The Prophet's breast is constricted by what opponents say as he bears revelation; inward bodily pressure and the obligation to voice the message are held together.
Moses says his breast constricts and his tongue does not move freely; the body under pressure is heard directly as difficulty in prophetic speech.
Moses calls Aaron more eloquent in tongue and asks that he be sent as vocal support, showing another person carrying part of a strained prophetic utterance.
Humanity labors toward its Lord with strenuous labor and will meet Him; the exertion of فَٱنصَبْ and the direction of فَٱرْغَبْ are fused in one Godward movement.
When the Quran is recited, listeners are told to attend and be silent; it supplies the receptive silence immediately before 7:205's quiet inward remembrance.
The angels glorify their Lord and prostrate without pride, completing 7:205's inward remembrance with worshipful praise.
Poets' wandering through every valley describes ungoverned imaginative speech, sharpening the controlled devotional exception in 26:227.
Poets are faulted for saying what they do not do, so the decisive boundary is between sound alone and speech embodied in action.
The Prophet is told to continue reminding, and the ayah clears him of being a soothsayer or mad; the next ayah adds the accusation of poetry.
Opponents call the reminding Prophet a poet, illustrating the very confusion between revealed dhikr and song-like utterance that 36:69 rejects.
